01 A field guide to an Ethereum collectible

Claim first.
Meet Pepe later.

A small guide to the free claim, the waiting, and the artwork that lives on-chain. Start here, even if this is your first NFT.

Explore the reveal ↗

No wallet. No signatures. Just learning.

The contract · Ethereum0x999ce0ce8c5f7661e0c74a568ffe27ceb9177bdb ↗Source reviewed · 29 Sep 2026

01 / Before the pixels

From eligible to yours.

An NFT is a unique token recorded on a blockchain. “Minting” creates that token; “revealing” makes its final artwork visible.

01

Be on the list.

The contract owner assigns each wallet an allowance of up to 3 claims. Owning an IMD NFT or paying for a swarm job does not automatically grant eligibility in the code.

Contract: grant / grantEach ↗
02

Free means mint price.

The claim has no mint payment. A real Ethereum transaction still costs gas, paid in ETH. The no-argument claim() takes your entire remaining allocation, not just one.

Contract: claim / _claim ↗Ethereum: gas fees ↗
03

Wait, then reveal.

A claim records the minter and mint block. The artwork seed uses the next block’s hash—a fingerprint of a block that does not yet exist at mint time.

Contract: _claim / reveal ↗
What else can stop a claim?+

Minting must be open, the caller cannot be the contract owner, and the request must fit the wallet’s allowance, its lifetime limit of 3, and the collection limit of 5,000. A partial allocation can be claimed through claim(amount). Transferring a Pepe away does not reset the mint count. These are code limits, not a report of current availability. Source: remaining, _claim, MAX_SUPPLY ↗

Creator’s statement

In a 25 September 2026 memo, the creator described an initial list of IMD NFT snapshot holders and swarm customers, with more wallets to be selected later. That is the creator’s selection policy; the contract enforces the allowance it is given. Read the original memo ↗

The order is the point.

You committed first. The missing input arrived later. Resetting creates a separate pretend experiment; a real revealed token cannot be rerolled. Contract: reveal ↗

A model, not a mint. All tokens, hashes and artwork here are invented. This uses a toy mixing function, not the contract’s keccak256 or actual trait probabilities. Nothing is sent to Ethereum. Real token IDs are assigned by the contract, not selected from this menu. Source: _claim / reveal ↗

What the code guarantees

A mint in block B targets B+1 and can first reveal at B+2. The seed combines that hash, the token ID, the original minter and this contract’s address. Anyone can trigger the reveal, and a stored seed stays fixed. Source: reveal ↗

What the demo doesn’t prove

It shows why an ordinary minter cannot preview the final traits at mint time. It does not prove perfect randomness or rule out influence by block producers. The creator’s stronger anti-grinding claim is not a security audit. Solidity’s randomness warning ↗

Will the reveal always happen automatically?+

The creator says a bot handles reveals. The contract itself needs a reveal transaction; it cannot schedule one. Anyone may call it, so it is not restricted to the creator or the token owner. A bot’s availability has not been checked here. Creator memo ↗ · Contract: reveal / revealableAt ↗

The contract’s Blockhash helper can use Ethereum’s extended history (up to 8,191 blocks), beyond the native 256-block window. If the fixed target hash is unavailable, the token stays unrevealed; there is no substitute hash or reroll. A timely reveal matters. Source: Blockhash.sol / reveal ↗

03 / No image server needed

The pixels live
with the code.

The token’s tokenURI returns its description and image as embedded data. The image is an SVG: a picture drawn from shapes, rather than fetched from an image server. Contract: tokenURI ↗

A separate on-chain PixelArt contract turns the seed into a 24 × 24 grid of colored rectangles. Skin, eyes, mouth, hat and accessory all come from that seed. Swarm Pepe’s reference to this renderer is fixed at deployment. PixelArt: renderSVG / attributes ↗SwarmPepe: immutable ART ↗

↳

In plain language: the contract contains the recipe for the picture. A marketplace displays that picture; it does not supply the artwork file.

04 / Check the field notes

Facts deserve footnotes.

Code describes the rules. A creator’s memo describes intentions. This guide keeps the two separate.
